name: Subadditivity Effect
description: When an event is unpacked into specific parts, the summed judged probabilities of those parts can exceed the judged probability of the broader whole. Detailed breakdowns can therefore feel more likely than the same outcome described in a packed, generic way.
design_relevance_note: Highly relevant to survey wording, risk communication, roadmap estimation, and option framing: the way scenarios are decomposed changes perceived likelihood, which can skew prioritization and forecasting.
prevalence_note: Well known in judgment-under-uncertainty and survey-methods research, but rarely named outright in mainstream product or UX practice outside advanced research/statistics discussions.

findings.description: Support theory predicts and demonstrates subadditivity in probability judgment: unpacking a broad event into explicit, specific components raises the summed judged probability of those components above the judged probability of the packed whole, because description changes perceived evidential support.
findings.source_title: Support theory: A nonextensional representation of subjective probability.

findings.description: Two experiments found subadditivity in frequency judgments (splitting a category into subcategories increases summed subjective frequency) varies systematically with the extremity and reliability of the underlying frequency estimate -- more extreme and less reliable estimates produce larger subadditivity effects. Proposes an independent, purely statistical (regression-to-the-mean) account of the phenomenon, distinct from Tversky & Koehler's support-theory explanation, while still confirming the base effect itself. A genuinely different theoretical mechanism converging on the same real phenomenon, with new moderators this corpus didn't previously have.
findings.source_title: On splitting and merging categories: a regression account of subadditivity
